name: Avicenna
info: Ibn Sina, known in the West as Avicenna, a Persian philosopher and physician of the Islamic Golden Age who served Iranian courts and wrote The Canon of Medicine and The Book of Healing.

facts.born: c. 980, in the village of Afshana near Bukhara in Transoxiana, to a Persian family; his father Abd Allah, of Balkh, was a Samanid official
facts.died: 22 June 1037, in Hamadan, of a severe colic contracted while accompanying Ala al-Dawla on campaign; buried in Hamadan
facts.role: Physician to the Samanid Nuh II from the age of 17; in the service of the Khwarazmshah at Gurganj; court physician to the Buyid Majd al-Dawla at Ray; vizier of Shams al-Dawla at Hamadan until 1021; adviser to the Kakuyid Ala al-Dawla at Isfahan
facts.known: The Canon of Medicine; The Book of Healing; the distinction between essence and existence; the 'Proof of the Truthful' for God's existence; the 'floating man' thought experiment; Peripatetic philosophy in the Muslim world

t: Avicenna wrote his works while moving between the courts of Iranian rulers as physician, administrator and vizier, at times in hiding or in prison.
His Canon of Medicine became a standard medical text in the Islamic world and at many European universities, and in Europe he was ranked with Hippocrates and Galen.

His philosophy, built on Aristotle and al-Farabi, distinguished essence from existence and argued for a Necessary Existent identified with God; al-Ghazali and other Islamic scholars condemned parts of it as unbelief.
dyk: Of about 450 works Avicenna is believed to have written, around 240 survive, including 150 on philosophy and 40 on medicine, and almost half of his works are in verse.
ev: Avicenna is born at Afshana near the Samanid capital Bukhara
The Samanid Empire falls, and Avicenna may have left for Gurganj in Khwarazm about this time
Avicenna enters the service of the Buyid amir Majd al-Dawla at Ray
His patron Shams al-Dawla dies, and Avicenna goes into hiding at Hamadan
The Ghaznavids briefly occupy Isfahan, and Avicenna leaves with Ala al-Dawla for Khuzistan
Avicenna dies at Hamadan after falling ill on campaign

sections.early:
Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Abdallah ibn Sina, known in the West by the Latinised form Avicenna, was born in about 980 in the village of Afshana in Transoxiana, near the Samanid capital Bukhara, his mother's home town. His father Abd Allah, a native of Balkh, was a Samanid official who had governed a village of the royal estate of Harmaytan under Nuh II. The family soon settled in Bukhara, a centre of learning that, under the Samanids, rivalled Baghdad as the cultural capital of the Muslim world.

Avicenna's father and brother converted to Isma'ilism, but he remained a Hanafi Sunni, the school of the Samanids, and later said he was 'unconvinced' by Ismaili missionaries. His parents hired tutors in Arabic and Islamic learning. By the age of 10 he had memorised the whole Quran; an Indian greengrocer taught him arithmetic, and the Hanafi jurist Ismail al-Zahid taught him law.

His father then brought the physician and philosopher al-Natili to teach him. Together they read Porphyry's Isagoge and possibly Aristotle's Categories, and after Avicenna had read Ptolemy's Almagest and Euclid's Elements, al-Natili told him to carry on alone. By 18 he was well versed in the Greek sciences. His autobiography names only al-Natili as a teacher, but he most likely also studied with the physicians Qumri and Abu Sahl al-Masihi.
sections.rise:
At 17 Avicenna was made a physician of the Samanid ruler Nuh II. When his father died, by the time Avicenna was at least 21, he received an administrative post, possibly his father's governorship of Harmaytan. He then moved, by his own account from 'necessity', to Gurganj, capital of Khwarazm, where through the minister Abu'l-Husayn as-Sahi he served the Ma'munid Khwarazmshah Abu al-Hasan Ali. The date is uncertain; he may have left in 999, when the Kara-Khanids took Bukhara and the Samanid Empire fell. Gurganj had become a centre of learning, where he joined his old teacher al-Masihi and the mathematician Abu Nasr Mansur.

In 1012 he moved west again, through the cities of Khurasan, hoping to serve the Ziyarid ruler Qabus of Gorgan, a patron of letters, but found him dead. At Gorgan he met Abu 'Ubayd al-Juzjani, who became his pupil and companion and later his biographer.

In about 1014 he went to Ray and served the Buyid amir Majd al-Dawla and his mother Sayyida Shirin, the realm's de facto ruler, as court physician, treating the amir for melancholia. In this period he finished The Canon of Medicine and began The Book of Healing. He then moved to the service of the rising Buyid amir Shams al-Dawla at Hamadan, who called him to treat him and then forced him to become his vizier.
sections.deeds:
Avicenna's Canon of Medicine is a five-book medical encyclopedia, covering general principles, medicinal substances, diseases and treatments, the keeping of health and specific ailments. In it he associated invisible tainted organisms with disease and recommended isolating the sick. It became the standard medical textbook in the Islamic world and Europe, and still plays a part in Unani medicine. He also recognised the contagious nature of tuberculosis, described a symptom of carotid sinus hypersensitivity and linked feelings to the pulse.

The Book of Healing, an encyclopedia of logic, natural science, mathematics and metaphysics, aimed to 'heal' the ignorance of the soul. In it he wrote on the formation of mountains over long periods, set out a method of experimentation (tajriba) beside Aristotle's induction, developed a theory of motion in which a thrower gives a projectile an inclination (mayl), and argued that the speed of light must be finite. His Danishnama, written in Persian for Ala al-Dawla, created a scientific vocabulary that had not existed in that language.

In metaphysics, following al-Farabi, he distinguished essence (mahiya) from existence (wujud) and argued that contingent things need a cause of their existence, leading to a Necessary Existent, one and without genus, whom he identified with God; Peter Adamson calls this 'Proof of the Truthful' his biggest contribution to philosophy. In prison at Fardajan he wrote the 'floating man' thought experiment, arguing that the soul knows itself apart from the body.
sections.opponents:
Avicenna's life at court was full of rivals and danger. At Hamadan in 1015 he debated Abu'l-Qasim al-Kirmani of the Baghdad school of philosophers; Avicenna accused him of ignorance of logic and Abu'l-Qasim accused him of rudeness. Abu'l-Qasim later made accusations so serious that Avicenna asked the amir's deputy to investigate; they may have been the charge, made earlier by the people of Hamadan, that he had imitated the style of the Quran in his Sermons on Divine Unity, an accusation whose seriousness, in the historian Peter Adamson's words, 'cannot be underestimated'. As vizier he sometimes clashed with Shams al-Dawla's troops.

After 1021, suspected by the Buyid court and its Kurdish vizier Taj al-Mulk of corresponding with the Kakuyid ruler of Isfahan, he was arrested at the house of his patron Abu Ghalib al-Attar and held for four months in the fortress of Fardajan; al-Juzjani blamed an informer.

His philosophy drew lasting criticism. Al-Ghazali, in Deliverance from Error, held that the Greek philosophers 'must be taxed with unbelief, as must their partisans among the Muslim philosophers, such as Avicenna and al-Farabi', and divided their teaching into unbelief, innovation and what need not be rejected. Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya also criticised his theology. In Latin Europe a 'Latin Avicennism' was suppressed by the Paris decrees of 1210 and 1215. Some of his science failed: his explanation of the rainbow was wrong, and modern scholars doubt that he could have seen the transit of Venus he claimed.
sections.last:
Avicenna was freed from Fardajan when Ala al-Dawla Muhammad, the Kakuyid ruler of Isfahan, captured Hamadan and ended the reign of Sama' al-Dawla. He went to Isfahan, where Ala al-Dawla gave him, in al-Juzjani's words, 'the respect and esteem which someone like him deserved'. Adamson calls his service there the most stable period of his life. He was Ala al-Dawla's adviser, if not his vizier, and went with him on many military expeditions and journeys.

When the Ghaznavids briefly occupied Isfahan in January 1030, Avicenna and Ala al-Dawla withdrew to Khuzistan in south-western Iran, staying until the death of the Ghaznavid ruler Mahmud two months later. On returning to Isfahan he seemingly began his Pointers and Reminders. He dedicated two Persian works to his patron, the Danish-nama-yi Ala'i and a treatise on the pulse.

He had suffered from colic all his life. In 1037, while accompanying Ala al-Dawla to a battle near Isfahan, he contracted a severe colic, and he died shortly afterwards, on 22 June 1037, in Hamadan, where he was buried. Avicenna's own autobiography, supplemented by a biography written by his pupil al-Juzjani, is the account on which the story of these years rests.
sections.legacy:
In the Islamic world Avicenna became, in Robert Wisnovsky's words, 'the central figure in the long history of the rational sciences in Islam', read, taught and commented on by thousands of later scholars in philosophy, medicine, theology and law. His theological views formed part of the core of the madrasa curriculum until the 19th century. Later readers divided: al-Tusi applied his system as a whole, al-Razi read his theological works on their own, an approach that came to prevail in the madrasas, and al-Ghazali used parts of it for mystical ends. His logic, developed by al-Katibi, became the dominant system of Islamic logic until modern times.

In Europe, the Canon, after its Latin translation, made him from the early 14th to the mid-16th century one of the acknowledged authorities in medicine, ranked with Hippocrates and Galen as princeps medicorum, 'prince of physicians'; the Canon remained in use at European universities as late as 1650. His psychology influenced William of Auvergne and Albertus Magnus, and his metaphysics Thomas Aquinas. Dante placed him in Limbo among the virtuous non-Christians.

Peter Adamson calls him 'the single most influential medieval philosopher' and the only medieval thinker with a significant influence on Islam, Judaism and Christianity. A lunar crater, Bu-Ali Sina University and UNESCO's Avicenna Prize bear his name, and Noah Gordon's novel The Physician (1988) made him a character.

summary: Avicenna (Ibn Sina), born near Bukhara about 980, served Iranian rulers as physician, administrator and vizier while writing The Canon of Medicine and The Book of Healing. His medicine dominated teaching in Islam and Europe for centuries and his philosophy of being shaped Islamic, Jewish and Christian thought, though al-Ghazali and others condemned parts of it.

notes: The article is inconsistent on when The Book of Healing was finished (1014-1020 in one section, completed at al-Attar's house after 1021 in another); no completion date is given.
It says he moved to Gorgan in 1012 but that Qabus had been dead since the winter of 1013; only 'found him dead' is used.
The Canon's use is given both 'as late as 1650' in Europe and 'up to the 18th century'; the 1650 figure is used with attribution.
A 'death of Mahmud two months later' is kept as the article gives it.
